segments.title: Reed, Watts, and two generations of HMS Monarch
segments.body: Edward Reed designed the 1868 Monarch and recruited the young Philip Watts into naval construction before resigning in July 1870 amid the HMS Captain dispute. Reed's engineering ability came with a difficult temperament. The Third Sea Lord regarded Reed's departure as a major loss to Royal Navy design. Watts later shaped Britain's dreadnought and Orion-class work, linking the two Monarchs through overlapping design teams. His approach to management distinguished minor mistakes, which subordinates or interfering officials could be allowed to discover for themselves, from decisions that endangered a ship or crew. For those more serious decisions, he retained responsibility.

evidence.note: Edward Reed's recruitment of Philip Watts, resignation in July 1870, and the distinction between minor design interference and decisions affecting safety.

segments.summary: The two ships named HMS Monarch connect Edward Reed's turret-ironclad work with Philip Watts and the Royal Navy's super-dreadnought era.

segments.title: HMS Captain, political pressure, and dockyard reform
segments.body: Captain Cowper Coles pressed for HMS Captain despite the objections of Edward Reed and Third Sea Lord Robert Spencer Robinson. First Lord Childers lost his son when Captain sank and blamed officials who had argued against the design. Monarch combined similar turret ideas with the seakeeping provisions that Reed and Robinson considered necessary. Robinson also helped develop a procurement case that treated potential enemies as serious enough to require a viable fleet without presenting them as unbeatable. In this interpretation, his dockyard and procurement reforms created capacity later used in the dreadnought arms race.

evidence.note: Coles's turret-ship proposal, Reed and Robinson's objections, Childers's reaction to his son's death, and Robinson's dockyard and procurement reforms.

segments.summary: Monarch emerged from the same turret-ship controversy as HMS Captain, while Robert Spencer Robinson's dockyard reforms prepared the Royal Navy for later expansion.

segments.title: Monarch's hull proportions and the uncertainty in length-to-beam ratios
segments.body: Monarch's length-to-beam ratio lay roughly between 5.5 and six to one, giving her unusually fine hull proportions for the period. One calculation gives 5.55, alongside published or personal estimates of 5.7 and 5.65. Including the ram bow in the measured length is one possible reason for the difference. Hull proportions affect resistance and how effectively engine power produces speed, although a fine hull is not necessarily easy to manoeuvre. Dreadnought's later ratio of roughly six to one provides a comparison with later battleship designs.

evidence.note: Length-to-beam estimates of 5.55, 5.7 and 5.65, possible ram-bow measurement differences, and the relationship between hull proportions, power, speed and manoeuvrability.

segments.summary: Estimates differ slightly for Monarch's length-to-beam ratio, while her fine hull favoured efficient use of engine power.

segments.title: Why twelve-inch muzzle-loaders needed such large turrets
segments.body: Monarch carried four twelve-inch rifled muzzle-loading guns. A barrel length of about 145 inches, or 3.7 metres, made reloading a problem of space as well as effort. The estimated withdrawal and muzzle clearance required roughly 4.5 to five metres before the gun returned to its firing position. Without sufficient space inside, loading would require work outside the turret. These demands help explain the bulky turrets and slow firing cycle of early heavy muzzle-loading weapons.

evidence.note: Four twelve-inch muzzle-loaders, approximately 145-inch barrels, and the estimated withdrawal and loading clearance inside a turret.

segments.summary: The length of Monarch's twelve-inch guns and the clearance needed at their muzzles explain why early turrets were bulky and slow to reload.

segments.title: Monarch's armour stayed while new machinery improved her speed
segments.body: Three seven-inch guns supplemented Monarch's main battery, later giving way to two nine-inch guns and one seven-inch gun. Her belt was about seven inches thick amidships and 4.5 inches towards the ends, while the turrets had ten-inch faces and eight-inch sides. Bulkheads were four to 4.5 inches thick, battle screens five inches, and the conning tower eight inches. New triple-expansion engines and boilers in an 1890 modernisation raised her powered speed from roughly 15 knots to nearly 15.75 knots, compared with about 13 knots under sail. The refit left the existing armour in place because replacing it was considered impractical. Twelve-pounder and three-pounder guns addressed the newer torpedo-boat threat.

evidence.note: Secondary-gun changes, armour thicknesses, new engines and boilers, speed figures, unchanged armour and light anti-torpedo-boat guns.

segments.summary: A machinery refit improved Monarch's speed and added light guns against torpedo boats while retaining her original armour.

segments.title: Why Monarch survived where HMS Captain failed
segments.body: Reed and Robinson accepted turret armament while rejecting the unsafe features of Coles's proposed implementation. Captain grew from a design of slightly under 7,000 tons to a completed displacement nearer 8,000 tons, aggravating the problem of weight and stability. Monarch kept her turrets closer together and carried higher freeboard, with more conservative provisions for seakeeping and safe operation. Captain was commissioned in April 1870 and lost in rough weather that September. Monarch was completed in June 1869 and survived until she was broken up in 1905, demonstrating that the turret concept could serve in an ocean-going ship.

evidence.note: Turret spacing, freeboard, Captain's growth from under 7,000 to nearly 8,000 tons, and the contrasting completion and service histories.

segments.summary: Monarch combined turret armament with higher freeboard and more conservative stability provisions, while Captain suffered substantial weight growth.

segments.title: Why reaching a target does not guarantee sustained air support
segments.body: Balanced forces depend on understanding what each service needs from the others. In the Libya example, aircraft flying from Britain could reach their targets with tanker support but had to return home to rearm after expending their weapons. Refuelling in flight could not remove that interruption, leaving gaps before another aircraft arrived. Apache helicopters operating from HMS Ocean illustrate the value of a nearby sea base for sustaining air support. Carriers and amphibious forces similarly allow sea power to support air and land operations, provided their capabilities are planned together.

evidence.note: The rearming limit of distant air operations, Apache operations from HMS Ocean over Libya, and cooperation between air, sea and land forces.

segments.summary: The Libya comparison shows why tanker support cannot replace a nearby base for rearming aircraft, and how HMS Ocean supported Apache operations.

segments.title: Forecastle, sail rig, and the limits of an early turret ship
segments.body: Reed disliked Monarch's forecastle because it obstructed forward fire, yet the Admiralty required it for seakeeping on long voyages. The sailing rig also interfered with turret arcs, and firing through the masts risked damage to the ship itself. Contemporary steam engines were not reliable enough for the Royal Navy to dispense with auxiliary sail on worldwide service. Raising the forecastle therefore added another restriction to an arrangement already constrained by masts. Monarch retained much of the hull form of a broadside ironclad while carrying turrets above it.

evidence.note: The Admiralty's seakeeping requirement, Reed's objection to the forecastle, mast interference with gunfire and Monarch's resemblance to a broadside ironclad.

segments.summary: Monarch's forecastle and sailing rig restricted forward fire but met the demands of global service with unreliable steam machinery.

segments.title: Larger guns favoured turrets before engines could free their firing arcs
segments.body: As naval guns grew heavier and more expensive, a full broadside battery became harder to accommodate and pay for. Turrets offered wider firing arcs for those heavy weapons. That advantage remained restricted while ships needed sailing masts as insurance against unreliable engines. Dependable triple-expansion machinery later made it possible to dispense with the sailing rig, with benefits beyond the increase in speed. The timing of a successful turret ship therefore depended on propulsion technology as well as the readiness of the guns and mountings.

evidence.note: Growing gun weight and cost, turret firing-arc advantages, retained masts and the role of dependable triple-expansion engines.

segments.summary: The weight and cost of larger guns encouraged turret armament, but reliable engines were needed before ships could dispense with obstructing sailing rigs.

segments.title: Why coastal turret ships could abandon sail sooner
segments.body: A harbour-defence ship could omit masts because it operated within reach of help. If its engines failed, another ship in company could tow it or a nearby base could send assistance. A Royal Navy warship expected to circle the globe could not depend on the same rescue arrangements. Auxiliary sail therefore remained useful on long voyages even when it compromised turret arcs. The acceptable risk of engine failure depended on where the ship would serve.

evidence.note: Engine-only turret ships near home bases could rely on towing or local assistance, unlike ships dispatched around the world.

segments.summary: Engine-only turret ships were more acceptable for harbour defence because a nearby base or another ship could provide help after a breakdown.

segments.title: Building Monarch modernized Chatham Dockyard
segments.body: Monarch's construction formed part of Chatham Dockyard's transition to modern industrial warship building. Robinson sought the dockyards' cooperation by giving them advanced ships to build and a reason to adopt new construction methods. He treated their early industrial experience as a foundation that needed updating as the fleet moved from sail to steam. His approach avoided setting the Royal Dockyards against private yards in a destructive rivalry.

evidence.note: Robinson's cooperative approach to dockyard modernisation, new construction techniques and the transition from sail to steam.

segments.summary: Robinson used advanced warship orders to win support for new construction methods in the Royal Dockyards.

segments.title: Why weaker French ironclads still mattered to a worldwide navy
segments.body: Robinson counted French wooden-hulled armoured ships as ironclads when making the case for British construction. Critics argued that this overstated the threat because British iron-hulled ships were individually more powerful. A concentrated battle between the two fleets was only one possible test of that advantage. French ironclads operating separately could threaten trade or blockade ports that Britain lacked enough armoured ships to protect. An ordinary unarmoured warship confronting one of those vessels would still face a serious disadvantage. Under those conditions, superior individual British ships would not remove the risk created by insufficient numbers. Continued construction also offered a way to pay for dockyard modernisation, a financial motive proposed alongside the operational argument.

evidence.note: Robinson's inclusive counting of French ironclads, criticism based on wooden hulls, and the conditional trade-raiding and blockade argument in defence of his threat assessment. The further suggestion that ship orders helped finance dockyard modernisation.

segments.summary: An ironclad inferior to its British counterpart could still threaten trade or ports elsewhere, making numbers relevant to global defence.

segments.title: Monarch as an ocean-going instrument of diplomacy
segments.body: Monarch's voyage with USS Plymouth and the remains of George Peabody combined diplomatic respect with a display of naval capability. Peabody's standing as an American financier and philanthropist gave the repatriation wider public significance. The American wooden screw sloop and the British turret ironclad offered a conspicuous contrast when they arrived together. Sending a modern capital ship across the Atlantic demonstrated Britain's ocean-going capabilities as part of a friendly gesture. A friendly Anglo-American gesture could also carry a competitive naval message. This was early in a career assessed at roughly 33 years of fighting usefulness, followed by three years as a depot ship.

evidence.note: Monarch's long service, the voyage with USS Plymouth for George Peabody's repatriation, and the interpretation of a friendly gesture with a competitive naval message.

segments.summary: Monarch's voyage with USS Plymouth honoured George Peabody while displaying Britain's ability to send a modern ironclad across the Atlantic.

segments.title: Monarch's 242-mile sailing day and the limits of record comparisons
segments.body: Monarch sailed 242 nautical miles in a single day, approaching HMS Ocean's reported 243-mile record. Ocean was a Prince Consort-class ironclad with an efficient hull, making her a useful comparison for Monarch's performance under sail. A difference of one mile was small against the uncertainty of measurements from the period. Using a rough margin of three percent either way, the two daily distances would be effectively indistinguishable. Monarch's fine hull had delivered a daily sailing distance comparable to Ocean's.

evidence.note: Monarch's 242-nautical-mile day, Ocean's 243-mile comparison and a suggested three-percent measurement margin.

segments.summary: Monarch came within one nautical mile of HMS Ocean's daily sailing record, a gap smaller than the rough measurement uncertainty suggested for the period.

segments.title: Collision, repair, and Mediterranean service
segments.body: In 1875 Monarch collided with the Norwegian barque Helven off Eddystone Rock, severely damaging both vessels. Repairs at Plymouth returned her to Mediterranean service in 1876. A 1877 refit addressed problems found in service, particularly the engine, while the boilers were considered satisfactory. She then resumed Mediterranean duty and remained there until 1885.

evidence.note: The 1875 collision, Plymouth repairs, return to the Mediterranean in 1876 and engine work in 1877, with the boilers considered satisfactory.

segments.summary: A collision off Eddystone Rock led to repairs at Plymouth, followed by Mediterranean service and an engine refit in 1877.

segments.title: Muzzle-loading gunnery at Alexandria
segments.body: At Alexandria, Monarch fired 125 twelve-inch shells at the forts, often as single aimed rounds. The total need not be divisible by four because the guns could fire individually. The accuracy was impressive for the period, although the engagement ranges were relatively short. One gun in the forward turret appears to have maintained a faster rhythm, possibly because it had an especially effective crew. Sustaining that volume of fire from heavy muzzle-loading rifles demanded considerable effort, and the crews were probably exhausted after the bombardment.

evidence.note: The 125-round total, single aimed shots, relatively short engagement ranges and the tentative identification of an especially effective forward-turret gun crew.
The physical effort of firing 125 heavy muzzle-loading shells and the expectation that gun crews would have been tired.

segments.summary: Monarch's 125 twelve-inch rounds at Alexandria included single aimed shots and unequal gun rhythms, with accuracy judged in the context of short ranges.

segments.title: How could loaders keep handling heavy six-inch shells?
segments.body: A viewer's comment raises the difficulty of repeatedly moving a roughly 50 kg six-inch shell, even for someone strong enough to lift one. Five or six sailors share the handling work, so no individual carries every round. After placing a shell, a loader can move into the next position without immediately carrying another. Those brief intervals allow some recovery while the crew continues working and help sustain the rate of fire. This example concerns six-inch shell handling, separate from Monarch's twelve-inch bombardment ammunition.

evidence.note: A viewer's concern about repeated six-inch shell lifting, with five or six loaders sharing the effort and taking intervals without carrying a shell.

segments.summary: Several loaders shared heavy-shell handling so that each man had intervals without carrying a shell while the crew continued working.
segments.question: How could a gun crew keep moving heavy six-inch shells without exhausting its loaders?
segments.answerShort: Five or six sailors shared the handling work, giving each man short intervals without carrying a shell even while the crew kept moving.

segments.title: Modernization carried Monarch into the twentieth century
segments.body: After a machinery breakdown on a passage towards Malta, Monarch continued under sail until she was taken in tow for repairs there. She then returned home under escort for more thorough work, followed by Channel service and repairs after HMS Minotaur collided with her. A major modernisation in the 1890s installed triple-expansion engines, after which she served as a guard ship at Simon's Bay until 1902. In March 1902, Captain Robert Carmichael Payne also held responsibility for Ascension Island. Under Captain William Lowther Grant, Monarch received Jan Smuts and Dennis Reitz on their way to a peace conference. By December 1902 she had become the Cape Town depot ship HMS Simoom. She remained useful even though her appearance was antiquated beside Royal Sovereign-style battleships.

evidence.note: Breakdown, towing to Malta, escorted return home, Minotaur collision, modernisation, guard-ship duty, command appointments, peace-conference passengers and depot service.

segments.summary: After breakdowns and collisions, new triple-expansion machinery helped the elderly Monarch remain useful as a guard ship and Cape Town depot ship.

segments.title: D. K. Brown and professional loyalties in naval history
segments.body: Alex Clarke reads D. K. Brown's design histories alongside copies annotated by his father, a fellow naval architect who knew and debated Brown. The marginal notes draw attention to professional disputes behind some portrayals of officers and constructors. Patronage networks and loyalties within naval construction could influence judgments about whose design advice deserved support. In this reading, Brown's factual work remains valuable while some interpretations reflect his experience of arguing with naval officers. That qualification informs the assessment of his account of Jellicoe and the Orion-class layout disputes.

evidence.note: Alex Clarke's recollections of Brown and his father's annotated books underpin the qualified criticism of Brown's treatment of design disputes.

segments.summary: Personal recollections and annotated copies of D. K. Brown's books raise questions about how professional disputes shaped later interpretations of warship design.

segments.title: Jellicoe's all-round view and the funnel-smoke problem
segments.body: Jellicoe wanted a gunnery-control position with a view around the ship, including astern. Mast placement also had to satisfy stability calculations and allow separation between the gunnery position and bridge structure. A mast's position relative to the forward funnel could leave smoke obstructing the view used for fire control. The intended arrangement relied on the ship moving fast enough to carry smoke aft while the elevated gunnery position remained above it. The disagreement involved assumptions about operating conditions as well as the physical placement of the mast.

evidence.note: The positions of the mast, boat deck, bridge and gunnery control, stability calculations, Jellicoe's view astern and the expectation that motion would carry smoke aft.

segments.summary: The Orion-class mast arrangement balanced all-round observation, separation from the bridge and stability against the danger of funnel smoke obscuring fire control.

segments.title: Sighting hoods and the limits of rearranging a ten-gun broadside
segments.body: Reginald Bacon insisted on sighting hoods as director of naval ordnance, and Archibald Moore continued the requirement after succeeding him. The hoods reflected contemporary gunnery knowledge and the equipment then available. D. K. Brown's criticism of the firing layout is contested on the grounds that the ship already had a ten-gun broadside. Moving the fifth turret farther forward or aft would concentrate other spaces amidships and depart from established British hull arrangements. Such changes also affected torpedo protection. Any proposed improvement still had to fit the infrastructure and budget available to build the ship.

evidence.note: Successive ordnance directors' requirement for sighting hoods, disagreement with Brown about firing layout, the fifth-turret alternative, torpedo protection and construction constraints.

segments.summary: Bacon and Moore's sighting-hood requirement and the difficulty of moving the fifth turret explain why improving Orion's layout involved competing demands.

segments.title: Why the Orion class kept the 13.5-inch gun
segments.body: The Orion class nearly received a larger gun than the 13.5-inch weapon eventually selected. An Elswick 14-inch/45 option was available, but it was less proven and fewer firms could manufacture it. The 13.5-inch gun offered lower development risk and a broader production base, and became a reliable weapon in service. Capital-ship procurement favoured reducing those risks because the consequences of failure included the lives of the crews.

evidence.note: The possibility of choosing a larger gun for the first generation of super-dreadnoughts.
The available Elswick 14-inch/45, its smaller manufacturing base and the preference for a more proven 13.5-inch weapon.

segments.summary: A proven design and a broader manufacturing base favoured the 13.5-inch gun over the available Elswick 14-inch/45 option.

segments.title: How a fourteen-inch Orion could have changed later gun choices
segments.body: A hypothetical move from twelve-inch to fourteen-inch guns changes the precedent for Britain's next increase in calibre. Repeating a two-inch step would give the Queen Elizabeth class sixteen-inch guns instead of the historical fifteen-inch battery. The same scenario extends to the R class, Renown, Repulse and Hood. A large British fleet of sixteen-inch ships would change the balance facing treaty negotiators if other navies retained only a few such vessels. The historical British progression was twelve-inch, 13.5-inch and fifteen-inch guns.

evidence.note: The hypothetical two-inch calibre progression, the named later British ships and the question of a treaty pause with unequal sixteen-inch fleets.

segments.summary: A counterfactual two-inch progression links the Orion gun decision to sixteen-inch later battleships and a different balance at the Washington negotiations.

segments.title: Monarch's machinery, trial speed and cruising range
segments.body: Armstrong Whitworth built Monarch at Elswick, with eighteen Yarrow boilers and two Parsons direct-drive turbine sets. Each turbine set drove two shafts, giving the ship four shafts in total. Designed for 21 knots, she achieved 21.9 knots on trials under safe operating conditions. Her fuel capacity supported more than 6,713 nautical miles at ten knots, with space to carry slightly more fuel than the standard provision. Her accurate guns are linked to the builder's emphasis on armament and obtaining the best performance from its installations.

evidence.note: Armstrong Whitworth construction, eighteen Yarrow boilers, two turbine sets driving four shafts, safe trial speed, fuel capacity and the assessment of gunnery quality.

segments.summary: Eighteen Yarrow boilers and Parsons turbines powered a ship that exceeded its 21-knot design speed and offered a cruising range above 6,713 nautical miles.

segments.title: Monarch's secondary guns and deterrent torpedo tubes
segments.body: Monarch carried sixteen four-inch guns and initially also had three-pounders. Three 21-inch torpedo tubes covered the two broadsides and the stern, with twenty torpedoes carried aboard. The arrangement allowed one torpedo to be fired on each of those bearings at a time, including a shot towards a pursuing ship. A single torpedo on a bearing offered a deterrent rather than the concentration of a larger torpedo attack.

evidence.note: Secondary guns, three 21-inch torpedo tubes, twenty torpedoes, firing bearings and the interpretation of single-torpedo fire as a deterrent.

segments.summary: Monarch's secondary battery included sixteen four-inch guns, while three torpedo tubes covered either broadside and the stern.

segments.title: Monarch's armour and early wartime fire-control and AA upgrades
segments.body: Monarch's protection included ten-inch barbette armour and eleven-inch turret armour. Deck armour varied between one and four inches, while the belt ranged from eight to twelve inches. By October 1914, sheltered guns had been enclosed in casemates and a fire-control director had been installed. A pair of three-inch anti-aircraft guns addressed both lighter-than-air and heavier-than-air threats early in the war. More armour followed Jutland without seriously reducing the ship's performance.

evidence.note: Barbette, turret, deck and belt thicknesses, October 1914 casemates, director and three-inch AA guns, and the limited performance effect of later armour.

segments.summary: Monarch accepted enclosed casemates, director fire control and AA guns by October 1914, followed by extra armour after Jutland.

segments.title: Why Monarch's exact construction cost is uncertain
segments.body: The quoted price for Monarch falls between £1.886 million and £1.889 million, but even this narrow range is difficult to resolve. Initial contracts and later modifications did not always enter the accounts in a way that makes the total clear. Historians and forensic accountants have struggled to reconstruct exactly what the Admiralty paid for individual battleships. Comparing a ship's cost with another figure therefore requires attention to what each total includes.

evidence.note: The quoted £1.886-1.889 million range and uncertainty caused by opaque Admiralty accounts, initial contracts and later modifications.

segments.summary: Competing cost figures for Monarch show how contracts, modifications, and opaque Admiralty accounting complicate comparisons between capital ships.

segments.title: How the Monarch design debate changed between 1868 and 1911
segments.body: Between the two Monarchs, naval architecture moved from debating the viability of an ocean-going turret ship to refining an accepted battleship arrangement. In the Orion-class debate, designers were no longer deciding between broadside and turret armament or proposing to abandon guns altogether. The comparison treats about ninety percent of the transition from the sailing broadside warship as already achieved, leaving disputes over the last ten percent of the arrangement. Those percentages express a judgment about the scale of change. The remaining decisions still provoked intense professional arguments because they concerned how closely an established design could approach its best fighting performance.

evidence.note: The contrast between making a new warship form viable and refining an accepted arrangement, expressed through the ninety-percent and ten-percent comparison.

segments.summary: The 1868 design asked whether a new warship form was possible; the 1911 design argued over how to perfect a form that had already completed most of its evolution.

segments.title: Why the second Monarch left service after only eleven years
segments.body: Monarch entered service in 1912 and left it in 1923, a much shorter career than that of her 1868 namesake. The First World War building programme left a supply of newer capital ships and reduced the need to retain the same depth of older hulls. Britain was no longer racing another navy ship for ship on the same basis. Competition over the quality of individual designs had existed before the war and continued afterwards. That strategic and material context helps explain the short service life of a ship otherwise judged sound.

evidence.note: Monarch's 1912-1923 service, the wartime supply of newer ships, reduced demand for older hulls and qualitative competition before and after the war.

segments.summary: Newer ships and reduced demand for fleet numbers shortened Monarch's career, while competition in the quality of warship designs continued.

segments.title: Why Monarch fired only 53 heavy shells at Jutland
segments.body: Under Captain George Borrett, Monarch was sixth from the head of the Grand Fleet's deployed line at Jutland. She fired 53 capped armour-piercing 13.5-inch shells and scored hits on König and Lützow, with possible hits on other ships left uncertain. British secondary batteries also opened fire when smoke suggested German torpedo boats were about to emerge. That different task required ammunition beyond the main-gun outfit. Smoke, limited engagement opportunities and the need to establish a firing solution restricted heavy-shell expenditure despite the hundreds of rounds carried. Observation and plotting had to precede firing, followed by assessment of the fall of shot and correction.

evidence.note: Command and fleet position, 53 capped armour-piercing shells, named hits and uncertain additional hits, secondary fire against a suspected torpedo threat, and the observation-and-correction cycle.

segments.summary: Monarch's heavy-shell expenditure at Jutland depended on visibility and firing opportunities, while a possible torpedo-boat threat brought secondary guns into use.

segments.title: Why loading speed did not determine the combat rate of fire
segments.body: The theoretical rate of fire measures how quickly a gun can discharge successive rounds. Combat firing also requires a target solution and corrections based on the observed fall of shot. Loading can continue while the fire-control team calculates the next shot, so some of the extra time needed for a larger shell overlaps with work required for both gun sizes. With comparable technology, twelve-inch and sixteen-inch guns can therefore achieve much closer practical rates than their loading figures suggest. The proposed dividing line in this explanation is 16.5 inches: above that size, loading can still delay firing after the calculations are complete.

evidence.note: Theoretical and realistic rates of fire, simultaneous loading and calculation, twelve-inch versus sixteen-inch guns with comparable technology and the proposed 16.5-inch dividing line.

segments.summary: Loading and fire-control calculations can overlap, bringing practical firing rates closer together than the mechanical rates of different gun sizes suggest.

segments.title: Advanced weapons need supporting systems ashore and afloat
segments.body: A weapon can be technically ready while the rest of the force remains unable to deploy or sustain it. Railguns and lasers require suitable power plants, ship infrastructure, dockside support and an industrial base. Missile development likewise depends on the infrastructure to sustain the weapons and load them at sea. Investment in the weapon itself can leave those supporting systems underfunded. Assessing readiness therefore requires examining the technologies and facilities needed to keep a weapon in service as well as its own performance.

evidence.note: The closing readiness questions, railgun and laser power and infrastructure needs, and the concern about missile sustainment and loading at sea.

segments.summary: Railguns, lasers and missiles require investment in power, ship systems and shore infrastructure before a navy can deploy and sustain them.

segments.title: Why Germany kept the torpedo-boat identity
segments.body: Before the First World War, the Imperial German Navy associated the destroyer with a defensive role. It wanted its torpedo craft to form an offensive fighting arm and retained more of the torpedo-boat identity in its terminology and outlook. The distinction depended on a contemporary perception of the ships' purpose. The later combat roles of Allied destroyers in the Second World War provide a conditional comparison: knowledge of those ships could have challenged the earlier defensive interpretation.

evidence.note: The German preference for an offensive torpedo arm, the contemporary perception of destroyers as defensive ships and a conditional comparison with later Allied destroyers.

segments.summary: The Imperial German Navy's emphasis on an offensive torpedo arm helps explain why it retained torpedo-boat terminology.
